extracted.intended_audience: academics and researchers (particularly in criminology/criminal justice) considering posting preprints
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rationale for posting journal-article preprints (public, time-stamped PDFs) to increase exposure and speed dissemination, plus practical steps for hosting and preparing files. Targeted at researchers deciding whether and how to post preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased exposure (avoid paywalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main benefit of posting preprints is to get your work more exposure. Traditional peer-review work is often behind paywalls which prevents the majority of non-academics (and sometimes other academics) from accessing your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting a preprint makes work accessible to practitioners and academics who won't go through inter-library loan or paywall hurdles. Note: to be influential broadly you still need non-academic writing/presentation, but preprints capture some otherwise-missed readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faster dissemination / timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: You get your work out much quicker via preprints than through the academic publishing cycle (which can take 6–12+ months from finish to online publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post when finished to avoid long delays; the author believes earlier and open versions on average double exposure compared to just the published version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post when ready (recommended timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically post papers either when doing a talk or when the paper is ready to go out for peer review; avoid posting really early drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it's good enough to send for peer review, it's appropriate as a preprint. This mitigates risks of sharing very early, unstable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for being wrong / ability to update
rubrics_metrics.description: If a preprint is wrong, take it down or update it; posting a version that will later be revised is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes peer review rarely causes substantive interpretation changes and you can update the preprint if peer review changes results; removing/updating is possible though not always straightforward in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of changing conclusions after peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Content may change after peer review (e.g., robustness checks, framing, discussion), but substantive interpretation changes are uncommon based on the author's experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can update the preprint with new results; acknowledge the (small) risk that early findings could be picked up and later invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scooping and priority / timestamp protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints provide a time-stamped example of your work which can prevent direct plagiarism and establish priority; risk of someone taking your idea and rewriting it remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This risk is most relevant for secondary data analysts; presenting at conferences carries similar risks. Preprints should at least make later citers more likely to cite your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals' and reviewers' attitudes toward preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Most journals in the (author's) field do not forbid preprints; reviewers may occasionally view preprints negatively but this is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If concerned, email the editor for clarification. An occasional reviewer may cite preprint posting as a negative, but editors who read reviews should recognize it's not substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity concerns in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting a preprint may reveal author identity and could influence double-blind review, but in many fields this is already moot (conference presentations, small field, reviewers can guess).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The anonymity risk may have small marginal effects that do not outweigh benefits for most situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low time/effort cost to post
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting a preprint involves simply uploading a PDF to your website or a hosting service; overall it takes very little extra work compared to current practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author describes a practical workflow: maintain components in Word, export to PDFs, and stitch with a tool like PDFtk to create a single CombinedPaper.pdf for upload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical workflow for preparing files
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep components (title page, main paper, tables/graphs, appendix) as separate files, export to PDF, and combine them (e.g., pdftk.exe TitlePage.pdf MainPaper.pdf TablesGraphs.pdf Appendix.pdf cat output CombinedPaper.pdf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a bat file to automate combining so updating the PDF is a double-click operation; note the author seldom uses LaTeX and prefers this Word+PDF workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hosting platform choices and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Public hosting options include posting on your webpage or services like Academia.edu, SSRN, and SocArXiv; SocArXiv preferred by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SocArXiv doesn't require co-authors to create accounts and is free to download; SSRN and Academia.edu often require sign-ups which create access hurdles, and Academia.edu has problematic terms of service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader open-science practices to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints are one piece of open science; other components include sharing replication materials/data and open peer-reviewed journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests treating preprints alongside other open-science practices and notes they'll write about replication materials/data sharing separately.
